newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain strippable debt seen attracting high demand.
newsitem.headline: Spain strippable debt seen attracting high demand.

text.p: Spain's first ever issue of strippable debt should be a big success at auctions on Tuesday and Wednesday this week, dealers said on Monday.
Invstors should be attracted to the new issue because the bonds will be exempt from witholding tax, though the secondary market could be a bit weaker in anticipation.
The dealers also expected global demand would be high enough to replace an unusually high level of maturing Spanish debt.

"The Spanish Treasury is interested in giving these new issues the highest possible degree of liquidity, and the new bonds are a good investment because they do not require the payment of the (25 percent) withoulding tax," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.

The new strippable debt will not have to pay the 25 percent witholding taxes when bought by Spanish institutional investors. Foreign investors have not paid witholding taxes on Spanish bonos since 1991.

Despite a positive opening on Monday, the first effect on the secondary cash and futures market is expected to be negative, dealers said. At 0745 GMT the long bond future had gained 20 basis points at 116.98, tracking a positive Italian debt market.

"It's mostly domestic-driven demand. But the new issues are expected to be cheaper than the outstanding ones, so the final effect is that investors will buy at the auctions, covering themselves, and sell the long-bond future," a trader said.
On Tuesday and Wednesday, the Spanish Treasury will offer three-, five-, 10-, and 15-years bonds, strippable for the first time ever.
The amount to be offered by the Spanish Treasury will not be known until later on Monday and dealers suspect it will be high as the Treasury needs every peseta it can get.

On Saturday, 760 billion pesetas ($5.2 billion) of newly cleansed black market money instruments matured. The instruments, which rendered the investors immune from tax evasion charges, were launched in 1991 to flush out undeclared black market earnings.
"Including everything from special debt to bills, the Treasury has to face in July maturing debt for 2.8 trillion pesetas," said Maria Victoria Nunez, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
Dealers said the Treasury's proposal to start new strippable issues, the coupons of which can be stripped off and traded separately, was very good.
"People expect these new issues to pay a bit of a premium, and so to be welcomed," she added.
The new bonds will not be strepple however until the volume outstanding reaches at least a trillion pesetas and the Treasury authorises an issue as strippable. This could take several months.
But the longer term effect on the market should be positive as it could reduce yields on Spanish debt.
"There is the idea, for example, that French yield spread over Bunds is negative because of that -- French bonds are strippable and Bunds are not, yet," said Valentin Fernandez.
